premises.content: A finite-hyperbolic-lattice construction used for numerical studies is implemented as follows: starting from a central polygon, perform n epochs of layer-by-layer inflation (adding neighboring regular p-gons at each outer edge) to produce N lattice sites such that each lattice vertex has coordination number q; then take the set of sites in the outermost (nth) layer and reconnect them among themselves by choosing a random matching of boundary bonds subject to the hard constraint that every boundary site retains degree q. This randomized reconnection of outermost-layer sites preserves the local vertex coordination q, suppresses boundary-dominated spectral and wavefunction features that arise under simple open-boundary conditions and that prevent observation of a bulk Anderson transition in small samples, and yields finite-size hyperbolic lattices whose bulk statistical properties (spectral statistics and wavefunction measures) move continuously toward those of the random regular graph (RRG) of degree D=q as the polygon-side parameter p (the number of sides of the regular polygon in the {p,q} tiling) is taken to the infinite limit p→∞.

steps.reasoning: Start from the finite hyperbolic lattices built with inflation and randomized outer-boundary reconnection, which preserve local coordination $q$ and reduce boundary artifacts. Consider the single-particle tight-binding Hamiltonian $H=\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle}t(c_i^\dagger c_j+\mathrm{h.c.})+\sum_j\epsilon_j c_j^\dagger c_j$, with hopping $t=1$ and onsite disorder $\epsilon_j$ uniformly distributed in $[-W/2,W/2]$.

To diagnose localization, the energy spectrum is divided into 10 equal segments and two observables are evaluated in each segment: the ratio of consecutive level spacings $r_i=\frac{\min(\delta_i,\delta_{i-1})}{\max(\delta_i,\delta_{i-1})}$ with $\delta_i=E_i-E_{i-1}$, and the inverse participation ratio $\mathrm{IPR}=\sum_j|\psi_{m,j}|^4$ for an eigenstate $|\psi_m\rangle$ with spatial amplitudes $\psi_{m,j}$.

For intermediate disorder, the energy-resolved averages $\langle r\rangle$ and $\langle\mathrm{IPR}\rangle$ separate the spectrum into distinct regions: the central-energy states remain in the extended regime, while the states near the spectral edges move into the localized regime. This produces side regions with localized behavior and a central region with extended behavior.

Because the transition point differs between the band center and the band edges, the energy dependence of the diagnostics implies a mobility edge, namely an energy-dependent boundary between localized and delocalized states. This is explicitly observed for the $\{3,8\}$ and $\{4,8\}$ lattices.

As disorder increases further, the energy-resolved statistics show that the extended central band also becomes localized, so the whole spectrum eventually reaches Anderson localization at sufficiently large $W$. Thus the system exhibits mobility edges at intermediate disorder and full localization at strong disorder.

motivating_questions.content: The spectral structure of disordered lattices is characterized by whether eigenstates at a given energy are localized or extended; in Euclidean lattices mobility edges occur in three dimensions and above, while in 1D/2D uncorrelated disorder usually leads to localization at arbitrarily small disorder. For hyperbolic lattices the interplay of (i) exponentially growing coordination shells, (ii) finite boundary-to-bulk fraction, and (iii) abundant closed loops of varying sizes makes it nontrivial to predict whether mobility edges will appear and at what disorder scales. Prior to this work, it was unclear whether hyperbolic lattices behave like low-dimensional Euclidean systems (with no finite-threshold AT), like treelike RRG/Bethe models (finite-threshold AT), or show a mixed, energy-dependent coexistence of localized and extended states. Resolving whether mobility edges exist is essential for understanding transport, spectral statistics, and the possibility of energy-selective localization in experiments on synthetic hyperbolic platforms.

reasoning_chains.conclusion_text: The single-particle tight-binding model with nearest-neighbor hopping amplitude $t=1$ and independent on-site disorder $\epsilon_j\in[-W/2,W/2]$ exhibits an Anderson localization transition at strong disorder and energy-dependent mobility edges on finite approximants of hyperbolic lattices $\{p,q\}$. In particular, for the hyperbolic tilings $\{3,8\}$ and $\{4,8\}$ the spectral statistics (the averaged ratio of consecutive level spacings $\langle r\rangle$, where $r_i=\frac{\min(\delta_i,\delta_{i-1})}{\max(\delta_i,\delta_{i-1})}$ and $\delta_i=E_i-E_{i-1}$) and the average inverse participation ratio $\langle IPR\rangle=\langle\sum_j|\psi_{m,j}|^4\rangle$ both show a disorder-driven crossover from Wigner–Dyson-like level statistics and vanishing IPR (delocalized states) at small $W$ to Poisson statistics and finite IPR (localized states) at large $W$, with the transition occurring at disorder strengths that depend on the eigenenergy, i.e., mobility edges are present.

motivating_questions.content: In the study of localization on lattice systems one needs clear bulk diagnostics that distinguish localized and extended single-particle states and that are robust to finite-size effects. For Euclidean lattices this is often achieved by studying spectral statistics and IPR across system sizes with well-understood boundary conditions. On hyperbolic lattices, however, the exponential growth of site number with radius and the finite boundary-to-bulk ratio mean that naively computed spectrum statistics and IPR may be dominated by boundary-localized features and not reflect bulk physics. Prior to this work there was no explicit demonstration, using finite-size controlled diagnostics adapted to hyperbolic geometry, that disorder can induce a true bulk Anderson localization transition on hyperbolic tilings and, importantly, whether that transition is energy-dependent (i.e., accompanied by mobility edges). Establishing the existence (or absence) of bulk AL and MEs is a prerequisite for any subsequent characterization of criticality or for connecting hyperbolic-lattice results with known limits such as random regular graphs.

steps.reasoning:
The authors have established that for $\sigma=0.05$, eigenstates at the band edges are localized (conclusion 1). They construct the energy dispersion curve for $\sigma=0.05$ (Fig. 2), smoothed to represent an infinite system, and apply the $R^2$ localization criterion to identify localized states. In Fig. 2, localized states are indicated by hatched lines. The curve shows that only states at the very bottom and top of the band are localized; states near the Fermi energy $\varepsilon_F$ are extended.
Fig. 2

The authors then present results for a larger disorder $\sigma=0.10$. Fig. 3 shows the lowest eigenstate for $\sigma=0.10$. This state is approximately one third the breadth of the corresponding state for $\sigma=0.05$ (Fig. 1) and is localized over just a few atoms, with zero amplitude elsewhere. This indicates increased localization at the band edge with stronger disorder.
Fig. 3

The authors state: "As $\sigma$ is increased the number of localized states also increases. The regions of localization at the top and bottom of the band as shown in Figure 2 spread towards the Fermi energy." This observation is drawn from comparing the dispersion curve and localization patterns for the two disorder strengths. The implication is that the mobility edges—the energies separating localized from extended states—move inward from the band edges as disorder increases.

Thus, the authors conclude that for cellular disorder in a one-dimensional hydrogen ring with all neighbor interactions, increasing the disorder strength from $\sigma=0.05$ to $\sigma=0.10$ broadens the energy windows of localized states at both band edges, expanding them toward the Fermi energy. This demonstrates that mobility edges move inward with increasing disorder in a realistic one-dimensional system.

motivating_questions.content: In the Anderson model, the mobility edge—the energy separating localized from extended states—shifts with disorder, but this dependence had only been studied in simplified nearest-neighbor tight-binding systems. For a system with realistic interactions and a full Hartree-Fock electronic structure, the evolution of the mobility edge with disorder strength had not been established. Knowing whether the number of localized states grows smoothly or abruptly as disorder increases is crucial for predicting the onset of insulating behavior in disordered polymers.

reasoning_chains.conclusion_text: Under both periodic (PBC) and open (OBC) boundary conditions and for the symmetry classes studied (A, AIII, D^\dagger), introducing disorder produces three distinct regimes as disorder strength is increased: (I) an extended (delocalized) phase in which the inverse participation ratio (IPR) is small for all states and $N_{Loc}\approx0$, (II) a mobility-edge (partially localized) phase in which a finite fraction of eigenstates have large IPR (the study classifies a state as localized if $I_\alpha \ge 0.4$) while others remain extended, and (III) a fully bulk-localized phase in which $N_{Loc}\approx n$ and the local density of states (LDOS) shows localization in the bulk. These three phases are distinguished numerically by $W$, IPR($E$), $N_{Loc}$, LDOS, and the edge density of states $\rho_{edge}$ (under OBC). The transition from Region II to Region III coincides with the abrupt vanishing of $W$.

conclusion.content: For the non-Hermitian SSH chain with disorder in hopping and/or on-site potentials, under both periodic (PBC) and open (OBC) boundary conditions, three distinct phases emerge as the disorder strength increases, for symmetry classes A (no symmetry), AIII (sublattice symmetry), and \(D^\dagger\) (PT symmetry). These are: (I) an extended (delocalized) phase where the inverse participation ratio (IPR) \(I_\alpha = \sum_i |\psi_\alpha(x_i)|^4 / (\sum_i |\psi_\alpha(x_i)|^2)^2\) is small for all right eigenstates \(\psi_\alpha\) and the number of localized states \(N_{Loc}\) (states with \(I_\alpha \ge 0.4\)) is \(N_{Loc} \approx 0\); (II) a mobility-edge (partially localized) phase where a finite fraction of eigenstates have large IPR (\(I_\alpha \ge 0.4\)) while others remain extended; and (III) a fully bulk-localized phase where \(N_{Loc} \approx n\) (\(n\) is the number of lattice sites) and the local density of states (LDOS) \(\sum_\alpha |\psi_\alpha(x_i)|^2\) shows localization in the bulk. The three phases are distinguished by the real-space winding number \(W\) (computed from the polar decomposition of \(H-E_b I\) as \(W = \frac{1}{L'}\mathrm{Tr}'(Q^\dagger[Q,X])\), where \(L' = L-2l\), \(l=0.2L\), and \(Q\) from \(H-E_b I = MSN^\dagger\)), IPR as a function of energy, \(N_{Loc}\), LDOS, and (under OBC) the edge density of states \(\rho_{edge}\) (fraction of states localized at the first two lattice sites). The transition from Phase II to Phase III coincides with the abrupt vanishing of \(W\) (from 1 to 0).

premises.content:
Consider the non-Hermitian SSH chain of length \(L\) (number of lattice sites) with Hamiltonian \(H = \sum_j [ (t_1+\delta_1) c_{j,A}^\dagger c_{j,B} + (t_1-\delta_2) c_{j,B}^\dagger c_{j,A} + t_2 (c_{j,B}^\dagger c_{j+1,A} + c_{j+1,A}^\dagger c_{j,B}) + \Delta_1 c_{j,A}^\dagger c_{j,A} + \Delta_2 c_{j,B}^\dagger c_{j,B} ]\). The point-gap spectral topology is computed in real space by choosing a base energy \(E_b\), forming \(H-E_b I\), performing a singular value decomposition \(H-E_b I = M S N^\dagger\), defining \(Q = M N^\dagger\), and evaluating the polar-decomposition winding number
      $$
      W = \frac{1}{L'} \mathrm{Tr}'\bigl(Q^\dagger [Q, X]\bigr),
      $$
      where \(X\) is the position operator, \(\mathrm{Tr}'\) denotes the trace restricted to a bulk region of length \(L' = L-2l\) with \(l = 0.2L\) as a boundary cut-off. In the non-Hermitian topological phase of the clean system, \(W\) is integer-quantized. Under quenched disorder in the hopping (\(\delta_{1,2}^R\)) and/or on-site potentials (\(\Delta_{1,2}^R\)), \(W\) is self-averaging and remains quantized and non-trivial up to substantial disorder strengths. The abrupt change of \(W\) from 1 to 0 coincides with the transition from a partially localized (mobility-edge) phase to a fully localized phase, establishing \(W\) as a bulk diagnostic for disorder-driven localization.

None of these are independently verified by the paper, and each could affect the reported W values or the critical disorder strength. steps.reasoning: Treat the real-space winding number $W$ as established (from conclusion 1) and use it alongside localization diagnostics to classify disorder-induced phases.

Define the localization diagnostic quantities explicitly: for each eigenstate $\alpha$ with wavefunction amplitudes $\psi_\alpha(x_i)$, the inverse participation ratio is $I_\alpha = \dfrac{\sum_i |\psi_\alpha(x_i)|^4}{\left(\sum_i |\psi_\alpha(x_i)|^2\right)^2}$; classify a state as localized if $I_\alpha \ge 0.4$ and define $N_{Loc}$ as the number of such localized states; define the local density of states (LDOS) at site $x_i$ by $\sum_\alpha |\psi_\alpha(x_i)|^2$; define the edge density of states $\rho_{edge}$ as the fraction of eigenstates localized on the edge (here quantified using the first two lattice sites).
[55]

Report the three disorder-induced regimes observed under periodic boundary conditions (PBC): 
(I) Extended (delocalized) phase: $I_\alpha$ is small for all states and $N_{Loc}\approx 0$; LDOS is spatially uniform. 
(II) Mobility-edge (partially localized) phase: a finite fraction of eigenstates satisfy $I_\alpha \ge 0.4$ while others remain extended, so $0 < N_{Loc} < n$; IPR plotted versus $\Re(E)$ shows coexistence of low- and high-IPR states. 
(III) Fully bulk-localized phase: $N_{Loc}\approx n$ (almost all states localized) and LDOS shows localization in the bulk. These three regimes are identified numerically using $W$, IPR$(E)$, $N_{Loc}$, and LDOS, with representative plots shown that distinguish the three regions.
Fig. 5

Report the analogous three regimes under open boundary conditions (OBC): 
(I) Skin phase: most eigenstates are localized at an edge so that $\rho_{edge}\sim 1$ and LDOS is concentrated at the edge. 
(II) Mixed (partial skin) phase: a fraction of states remain edge-localized while others occupy the bulk, yielding $0<\rho_{edge}<1$ and an LDOS showing both edge peaks and bulk weight. 
(III) Bulk-localized phase: $\rho_{edge}\sim 0$ and LDOS shows localization in the bulk. These regimes are quantitatively distinguished by $\rho_{edge}$ and $W$, with LDOS panels illustrating Regions I, II and III.
Fig. 6

State how $W$ distinguishes the phases: under both PBC and OBC, the transition from Region II (mobility-edge / mixed) to Region III (fully bulk-localized) coincides with the abrupt vanishing of the winding number $W$; numerically this is seen as a sharp jump of $W$ from $1$ to $0$ at the disorder strength where $N_{Loc}$ becomes extensive (under PBC) or $\rho_{edge}$ goes to zero and edge LDOS disappears (under OBC).

Using a nearest-neighbor tight-binding Hamiltonian
$H=\sum_i E_i a_i^\dagger a_i+\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle} t_{ij}(a_i^\dagger a_j+h.c.)$
with explicit onsite energy disorder $E_i$ drawn from a Gaussian of width $s$ and positional disorder modeled by independent Gaussian site displacements of standard deviation $g$ (with $t_{ij}=t_0 e^{-\kappa\Delta d_{ij}}$), the localization character of single-particle eigenstates is diagnosed by finite-size scaling of the inverse participation ratio
$I_2[\Psi_n]=\sum_r|\Psi_n(r)|^4$,
extracting a fractal exponent $d_2$ via $I_2\propto L^{-d_2}$. States with $d_2\gtrsim 1.33$ are identified as localized while states with $d_2\lesssim 1.33$ are delocalized (the universal critical $d_2$ at the mobility edge). In the simple-cubic example with parameters $s/t_0=2.0$ and $\kappa g=0.2$, a symmetric miniband of width $\sim 12t_0$ forms centered at $E=0$, and mobility edges are found at approximately $E=\pm 6.8t_0$ separating delocalized miniband states from exponentially decaying band-tail localized states; deep-tail states show $d_2\approx 0$ while miniband-center states show $d_2\approx 2.67\approx 3$, consistent with extended states in 3D.

steps.reasoning:
State the microscopic model used to diagnose localization: the nearest-neighbor tight-binding Hamiltonian
$H=\sum_i E_i a_i^\dagger a_i+\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle} t_{ij}(a_i^\dagger a_j + \mathrm{h.c.})$, where $H$ is the Hamiltonian, $i$ and $j$ label lattice sites (nanocrystals, NCs), $E_i$ is the onsite single-particle energy of site $i$, $a_i^\dagger$ and $a_i$ are fermionic creation and annihilation operators on site $i$, $\langle i,j\rangle$ denotes nearest-neighbor pairs, and $t_{ij}$ is the hopping matrix element between sites $i$ and $j$. The simulation approach follows prior numerical implementations of tight-binding localization diagnostics. 
[28]

Specify the disorder models incorporated into the Hamiltonian and define all disorder parameters: onsite energy disorder is modeled by drawing each $E_i$ independently from a Gaussian distribution with standard deviation $s$, so $P(E_i=E)\propto e^{-E^2/(2s^2)}$, where $s$ (units of energy) quantifies size-inhomogeneity-induced energetic disorder; positional disorder is modeled by independent Gaussian displacements of each NC center with standard deviation $g$, so a site displacement component $\Delta x$ is drawn from $P(\Delta x_i=\Delta x)\propto e^{-\Delta x^2/(2g^2)}$, and the deviation of the edge-to-edge distance between neighboring dots is $\Delta d_{ij}=\Delta x_j^{(\alpha)}-\Delta x_i^{(\alpha)}$ for direction $\alpha$ from $i$ to $j$. The distance dependence of coupling is taken as $t_{ij}=t_0 e^{-\kappa \Delta d_{ij}}$, where $t_0$ is the coupling at the average distance and $\kappa$ is the inverse decay length parameter (units of inverse length).

Define the wave-function localization diagnostic and finite-size scaling procedure: for a single-particle eigenstate $\Psi_n(\mathbf{r})$ the inverse participation ratio (IPR) is computed as $I_2[\Psi_n]=\sum_r |\Psi_n(r)|^4$, where the sum runs over discrete lattice sites $r$ and $I_2$ measures inverse spatial extent. For a system of linear size $L$ in spatial dimension $d$ the scaling hypotheses are: (i) completely delocalized states occupy the whole system so $|\Psi_n(r)|\sim L^{-d/2}$ and $I_2\sim L^{-d}$; (ii) completely localized states occupy a finite region so $I_2\sim L^0$; and (iii) at the localization–delocalization transition wave functions are multifractal and obey $I_2\propto L^{-d_2}$ with $0<d_2<d$, where $d_2$ is the fractal exponent. These relations define $d_2$ operationally by fitting $I_2$ versus $L$ to a power law $I_2\propto L^{-d_2}$.
[41]

State the universal critical value used to distinguish localized from delocalized in 3D and how it is applied: previous numerical studies reported that at the Anderson localization critical point in three dimensions the multifractal scaling exponent is $d_2=1.33\pm0.02$. Therefore adopt $d_2\approx 1.33$ as the empirical mobility-edge criterion in 3D: states with $d_2\gtrsim 1.33$ are classified as localized (multifractal to localized side) and states with $d_2\lesssim 1.33$ are classified as delocalized (multifractal to delocalized side). Define the practical usage: compute $d_2(E)$ by fitting $I_2$ vs $L$ at fixed energy $E$ and use the $d_2(E)=1.33$ contour to locate mobility edges in $E$.
[41]

Describe the numerical procedure used to obtain $I_2$ and $d_2(E)$: generate ensembles of disordered lattices (Monte Carlo sampling of positional disorder displacements and independent draws of onsite energies), diagonalize the single-particle tight-binding Hamiltonian for finite cubic samples of several linear sizes $L$, compute eigenstates and their $I_2$, average $I_2(E)$ over disorder realizations in narrow energy bins, and for each energy bin fit the averaged $I_2$ versus $L$ to a power law to extract $d_2(E)$.
[28]

Apply the method to the simple-cubic (sc) example and report the quantitative findings and diagnostics: for the simple-cubic lattice (coordination number $N=6$) with dimensionless parameters $s/t_0=2.0$ (onsite disorder normalized by $t_0$) and $\kappa g=0.2$ (positional disorder in units of the decay parameter $\kappa$), the computed density of states (DOS) shows formation of a symmetric miniband centered at $E=0$ with bandwidth approximately $12t_0$; the DOS outside the miniband decays exponentially (band tails). Finite-size scaling of $I_2(E)$ yields $d_2(E)\approx 2.67$ near the miniband center (consistent with extended states in three dimensions where $d=3$), $d_2(E)\approx 0$ for deep tail states (consistent with fully localized states), and $d_2(E)\approx 1.24$ at energies near $E=7.0t_0$, which is close to the critical value $d_2\approx 1.33$. From the $d_2(E)=1.33$ contour, mobility edges are located at approximately $E=\pm 6.8t_0$, separating delocalized miniband-center states ($|E|<6.8t_0$) from exponentially localized band-tail states ($|E|>6.8t_0$).
Fig. 1

Summarize the diagnostic outcome as an operational conclusion: combining the explicit disorder models, numerical diagonalization, IPR finite-size scaling, and the universal critical exponent $d_2\approx 1.33$ provides a reproducible workflow to identify mobility edges and to classify states as localized or delocalized in realistic NC assemblies; the simple-cubic example demonstrates that this procedure yields concrete mobility-edge energies in units of $t_0$ (here $\pm 6.8t_0$) and shows the multifractal behavior of states at the transition.
Fig. 1

motivating_questions.content: In NC solids one needs a reliable, quantitative criterion to decide whether electronic states are extended (permitting band-like transport) or localized (precluding coherent conduction). Prior analyses either treated disorder phenomenologically without positional disorder statistics or did not connect finite-size scaling diagnostics to phase boundaries applicable to realistic assemblies. Without an explicit calculation that (i) includes both realistic onsite energy distributions from size dispersion and positional fluctuations of NC centers, (ii) applies a finite-size multifractal/I_2 scaling analysis to extract the fractal exponent $d_2$, and (iii) identifies mobility edges in physical units of the coupling energy $t_0$, it is impossible to state when a given experimental NC solid will support delocalized states. This conclusion addresses that gap by providing a reproducible diagnostic workflow and concrete mobility-edge numbers for representative parameters.

reasoning_chains.conclusion_text:
Introducing onsite Anderson disorder
$$
\Delta H_{\mathrm{disorder}}=\sum_{n,i}\delta\mu_{i,n}\,c_{i,n}^{\dagger}c_{i,n},\qquad \delta\mu_{i,n}\in[-W,W],
$$
the numerical studies show that edge-localized states induced by a non-zero Pontryagin index remain exponentially localized and spectrally identifiable as long as the disorder amplitude $W$ remains below values that close the bulk principal gap; when disorder exceeds the gap scale the edge states dissolve into the bulk. The disorder protection therefore follows the expected gap-based stability of the introduced topological phases.

$$

$$
where each $\delta\mu_{i,n}$ is drawn independently from a uniform distribution in the indicated interval. This models uncorrelated Anderson disorder of strength $W$ added to the tight-binding Hamiltonian.

Report the numerical observation of edge-state stability up to gap closing and the disorder-induced dissolution beyond that: compute finite-size slab spectra and wavefunction profiles under open boundary conditions with disorder realizations at varying $W$. motivating_questions.content: In the physical context of finite closed-surface carbon quantum dots (fullerenes) under consideration (e.g., C60, C180), electronic eigenstates of the clean tight-binding model are spatially extended and possess degeneracies determined by icosahedral symmetry. Prior studies had not quantified how Anderson-type randomness localized those eigenstates in finite fullerenes at disorder strengths comparable to realistic perturbations (estimates $V_{\mathrm{on,off}}\sim 0.1t_{0}$ were suggested). Existing absence of such quantification left open whether eigenstate localization in realistic disorder regimes (moderate, experimentally plausible $V$) was strong enough to break inversion-related selection rules or to change charge distributions that feed into dynamical nonlinear response. Without a measure (such as the inverse participation number) across disorder types and sizes, one could not predict how disorder-modified eigenstate localization would alter interband dipoles, initial occupations, or subsequent strong-field dynamics and HHG spectra.

The order parameter used to distinguish localized versus extended states is the typical (geometric-mean) density of states (TDOS). The TDOS at energy $E$ is defined as
$\rho_{\mathrm{t}}(E) = \exp\!\left(\frac{1}{4 N_s}\sum_{i=1}^{N_s}\sum_{\sigma=1}^{2}\sum_{\tau=1}^{2} [\ln \rho_{i,\sigma,\tau}(E)]\right)$,
where $[\dots]$ denotes averaging over disorder realizations; $N_s$ selects a small set of sample lattice sites (with $N_s\ll L^3$ for a system of linear size $L$) to compute the geometric mean; and the local density of states (local DOS) at site $i$ for spin $\sigma$ and orbital $\tau$ is $\rho_{i,\sigma,\tau}(E) = \sum_n |\langle n|i,\sigma,\tau\rangle|^2 \delta(E-E_n)$ where $|n\rangle$ and $E_n$ are exact eigenstates and eigenenergies. When evaluating surface TDOS the sum over $i$ is restricted to lattice sites on the surface; when evaluating bulk TDOS the sum over $i$ is restricted to lattice sites in the system half closest to the center to avoid boundary effects.

The TDOS is computed numerically using the kernel polynomial method (KPM), which expands operators in Chebyshev polynomials up to an expansion order $N_c$ to approximate spectral quantities on very large lattices. The authors perform KPM computations on cubic lattices with linear size up to $L=100$, average over 5000 disorder configurations for TDOS computations, and treat the expansion order $N_c$ as the principal finite-resolution control parameter for KPM results; larger $N_c$ corresponds to finer spectral resolution and yields results closer to the thermodynamic $N_c\to\infty$ limit. This numerical setup permits separate evaluation of surface and bulk TDOS as functions of disorder strength $W$, energy $E$, system size $L$, and expansion order $N_c$. 
[89]
Fig. 2

The authors identify disorder-driven localization transitions by examining the behavior of the TDOS at the band center ($E=0$). They fit the TDOS near a transition to a power law of the form $\rho_{\mathrm{t},j}(E=0)\sim |W-W_{c,j}|^{\beta_j}$ for each sector $j\in\{S,B\}$ (surface $S$ or bulk $B$), using data for $W$ on the side where the TDOS is finite and vanishes approaching the transition. For a given KPM expansion order $N_c$ this yields estimates of $W_{c,j}(N_c)$ and $\beta_j(N_c)$ for that resolution.
Fig. 2

To remove finite-$N_c$ KPM resolution effects and obtain transition points and exponents in the infinite-resolution limit, the authors extrapolate the fitted $W_{c,j}(N_c)$ linearly as a function of $1/N_c$ to the limit $1/N_c\to 0$ (i.e., $N_c\to\infty$). Applying this linear-in-$1/N_c$ extrapolation to the fitted surface and bulk critical disorder strengths yields $W_{c,S} = 0.46 \pm 0.02$ and $W_{c,B} = 0.59 \pm 0.02$, demonstrating that the surface mobility edge closes at weaker disorder than the bulk mobility edge, i.e., $W_{c,S} \lt W_{c,B}$.

These $\beta_j$ values are the thermodynamic-limit geometric-DOS vanishing exponents associated with each mobility edge.

motivating_questions.content: In the study of disorder-driven topology, practitioners need reliable diagnostics and critical exponents to determine whether disorder localizes or delocalizes states on the surface and in the bulk independently. Prior analyses typically characterized disorder effects via bulk mobility-gap closures or by focusing on two-dimensional Chern models where only a single critical disorder strength exists; they did not provide a numerically controlled extraction of separate surface and bulk critical disorder strengths or corresponding critical exponents when a three-dimensional insulator has intrinsically gapped surfaces. Without such quantitative data one cannot establish whether surface and bulk localization transitions are concomitant or decoupled, nor can one assign them to known universality classes based on scaling exponents. The absence of this information prevents prediction of extended parameter regimes where surface conduction and topology differ from the bulk and obstructs comparisons to random-matrix and IQH universality classifications.

steps.reasoning: Define the localization length diagnostics used by the authors: the total localization length along $y$ is denoted $\lambda_y$, and the normalized localization length is $\lambda_y/N$ where $N$ is the linear sample size (number of primitive cells along each edge of the square sample). Finite-size scaling behavior is as follows: for a localized state $\lambda_y/N$ decreases with increasing $N$; for an extended (delocalized) state $\lambda_y/N$ increases with increasing $N$; at a critical (mobility edge) point $\lambda_y/N$ is independent of $N$. These finite-size scaling rules are the standard diagnostics the authors apply to distinguish localized from extended states and to detect mobility edges. [89-94]

Explain the difference between open and periodic boundary conditions (BCs) in the localization-length diagnostics and the rationale: open boundary conditions in the $x$ direction (and periodic in $y$) allow edge states to contribute to $\lambda_y$ whereas periodic boundary conditions in both directions eliminate edge contributions; comparing the disorder dependence of $\lambda_y$ under open and periodic BCs therefore isolates edge-related signatures (peaks present only for open BCs) from bulk-related signatures (peaks present under periodic BCs). The authors adopt this comparison to attribute specific localization-length features to edge or bulk physics. Fig. 7

Present the authors' numerical observation of an open-boundary, size-independent sharp peak marking edge band-gap closing: for parameters $m=t$, $\Delta_x=0.5t$, and $\Delta_0=0.4t$, the authors compute the total localization length $\lambda_y$ versus disorder strength $W$ under open boundary conditions and observe a pronounced peak at $W\approx3.1t$ whose position is independent of system size $N$; by contrast this peak is absent when periodic boundary conditions are used. The authors therefore identify the $W\approx3.1t$ open-BC peak as an unambiguous marker of the edge band-gap closing point, i.e., where edge states become gapless/fill the edge gap. Fig. 7(b)Fig. 7(c)

Link the open-BC peak to corner-state destruction using real-space wavefunctions: the authors compute disorder-averaged squared amplitudes of the corner-state wavefunction along the $y$ direction, $|\psi(i_x=1,i_y)|^2$ with $i_y\in[1,N]$, and find that these amplitudes spread out into the edge and the corner-state weight vanishes around the same disorder $W\approx3.1t$ where the open-BC $\lambda_y$ peak appears; simultaneously the quadrupole moment $Q_{xy}$ loses its quantization (drops from $0.5$ toward smaller values). From this correlation the authors infer that the edge-gap filling/closing at $W\approx3.1t$ causes the corner states to delocalize into the edge and disappear. Fig. 7(d)Fig. 7(a)

Describe the energy-resolved and system-size-resolved scaling that identifies bulk mobility gaps and their collapse: the authors compute the normalized localization length $\lambda_y/N$ as a function of energy $E$ for several system sizes $N$ and for a sequence of disorder strengths $W$ (plots shown for $m=t$, $\Delta_0=0$, $\Delta_x=0.5t$); these energy-resolved scalings reveal a mobility gap centered near $E=0$ for small to moderate $W$, with critical points (size-independent $\lambda_y/N$) marking mobility edges; as $W$ increases the mobility gap shrinks and eventually vanishes, and from these data the authors identify the bulk-mobility-gap collapse near $W\approx6.8t$--$7t$ for $m=t$, $\Delta_0=0$. Fig. 4

Summarize how these diagnostics allow separation of edge and bulk gap closings: (i) a sharp, system-size-independent peak in $\lambda_y$ under open BCs that is absent under periodic BCs identifies an edge band-gap closing (example $W\approx3.1t$ for $m=t$, $\Delta_0=0.4t$); (ii) the disappearance of energy-resolved mobility gaps detected by size-scaling of $\lambda_y/N$ identifies bulk mobility-gap collapse (example $W\approx6.8t$--$7t$ for $m=t$, $\Delta_0=0$); (iii) wavefunction spreading and $Q_{xy}$ loss coincident with the open-BC peak confirm that corner-state loss at the lower disorder is edge-driven while corner-state loss at the higher disorder is bulk-delocalization driven. The authors therefore conclude that localization-length scaling is an effective diagnostic to determine whether corner-state loss is driven by edge physics or by bulk delocalization. Fig. 7Fig. 4

motivating_questions.content: Discriminating whether corner-state disappearance under disorder arises from local edge-band filling (edge-gap collapse) or from bulk mobility-gap collapse requires diagnostics that are sensitive to boundary-localized physics. Global measures like the band-spectrum or bulk DOS alone cannot distinguish edge-driven versus bulk-driven transitions. Prior studies did not establish a simple, robust protocol (and its numerical thresholds) to separate these cases. Without such diagnostics one cannot reliably map phase diagrams or interpret numerically-observed loss of corner signatures in disordered samples.

Compute the normalized localization length $\\Lambda(E)$ as a function of energy $E$ by the transfer-matrix method with finite-size scaling: form the site transfer matrices $M_{n}$ from the discrete Schrödinger equation, multiply them to obtain the total transfer matrix $T_{N}=\\prod_{n=1}^{N}M_{n}$ while using Gram–Schmidt reorthonormalization to control numerical overflow, extract Lyapunov exponents from the limiting matrix $\\lim_{N\\to\\infty}\\ln(T_{N}T_{N}^{\\dagger})^{1/2N}$, and define $\\lambda$ as the reciprocal of the smallest positive Lyapunov exponent; then examine the $N$-dependence of $\\Lambda$ to distinguish extended states (where $\\Lambda$ increases with $N$) from localized states (where $\\Lambda$ decreases with $N$).
[28]

Observe via finite-size scaling of $\\Lambda(E)$ that a continuous energy interval of extended eigenstates exists for the long-range correlated single chain in the parameter regime studied; specifically, the finite-size scaling curves (system sizes $N$ varied from $2^{13}$ to $2^{16}$) show intersection behavior that identifies transition points between extended and localized behavior, indicating a band of extended states rather than isolated extended eigenvalues; this observation is displayed as the normalized localization length versus energy plot.

premises.content:
The collective small-amplitude dynamics of vortex cores in the Sierpiński carpet array is governed by a rotating-wave-approximation form of Thiele's equation,
      given by
      $$
      \begin{aligned}
      -i\dot{\psi}_j =& \left(\omega_0 - \frac{\xi_1^2 + \xi_2^2}{\omega_0}\right)\psi_j + \sum_{k\in\langle j\rangle,l} \zeta_l \psi_k - \frac{\xi_1\xi_2}{2\omega_0} \sum_{s\in\langle\langle j\rangle\rangle_1} e^{i2\bar{\theta}_{js}} \psi_s \\
      &- \frac{\xi_2^2}{2\omega_0} \sum_{s\in\langle\langle j\rangle\rangle_2} e^{i2\bar{\theta}_{js}} \psi_s - \frac{\xi_1^2}{2\omega_0} \sum_{s\in\langle\langle j\rangle\rangle_3} e^{i2\bar{\theta}_{js}} \psi_s,
      \end{aligned}
      $$
      where $\psi_j=u_j+iv_j$ is the complex displacement of the $j$th vortex core, $\omega_0=K/|G|$ with $K$ the single-disk spring constant and $G=-4\pi Q w M_s/\gamma$ the gyroscopic coefficient (with $Q$ the vortex topological charge, $w=10$ nm the nanodisk thickness, $M_s=0.86\times10^6$ A/m the saturation magnetization, and $\gamma$ the gyromagnetic ratio), $\zeta_l=(I_{\parallel,l}-I_{\perp,l})/2|G|$ and $\xi_l=(I_{\parallel,l}+I_{\perp,l})/2|G|$ are nearest- and next-nearest-neighbor coupling combinations for bond type $l=1,2$, $\langle j\rangle$ denotes nearest neighbors, $\langle\langle j\rangle\rangle_{1,2,3}$ denote the three distinct next-nearest coupling routes ($d_1\to d_2$, $d_2\to d_2$, $d_1\to d_1$), and $\bar{\theta}_{js}$ is the geometrical relative angle between sites.
      This dynamical equation is equivalent to a complex-valued tight-binding Hamiltonian
      $$
      \begin{aligned}
      \mathcal{H} &= \sum_{j}\left(\omega_{0}-\frac{\xi_{1}^{2}+\xi_{2}^{2}}{\omega_{0}}\right) \psi_{j}^{*} \psi_{j}+\sum_{\langle j k\rangle}\zeta\, \psi_{j}^{*} \psi_{k}-\frac{\xi_{1} \xi_{2}}{2 \omega_{0}} \sum_{\langle\langle j k\rangle\rangle_{1}} e^{i 2 \tilde{\theta}_{j k}} \psi_{j}^{*} \psi_{k} \\
      &\quad -\frac{\xi_{2}^{2}}{2 \omega_{0}} \sum_{\langle\langle j k\rangle\rangle_{2}} e^{i 2 \tilde{\theta}_{j k}} \psi_{j}^{*} \psi_{k}-\frac{\xi_{1}^{2}}{2 \omega_{0}} \sum_{\langle\langle j k\rangle\rangle_{3}} e^{i 2 \tilde{\theta}_{j k}} \psi_{j}^{*} \psi_{k}+ \text{c.c.},
      \end{aligned}
      $$
      in which the on-site term $\omega_{0}-(\xi_1^2+\xi_2^2)/\omega_0$ is nonzero and explicitly breaks chiral symmetry. The model parameters $I_{\parallel}(d)$ and $I_{\perp}(d)$ are the longitudinal and transverse magnetostatic coupling constants as functions of the dimensionless inter-disk distance $d$ (normalized by disk radius $r=50$ nm), given by $I_{\parallel} = \mu_0 M_s^2 r(-1.72064 \times 10^{-4} + 4.13166 \times 10^{-2}/d^3 - 0.24639/d^5 + 1.21066/d^7 - 1.81836/d^9)$ and $I_{\perp} = \mu_0 M_s^2 r(5.43158 \times 10^{-4} - 4.34685 \times 10^{-2}/d^3 + 1.23778/d^5 - 6.48907/d^7 + 13.6422/d^9)$.

If the configurations are generated as independent per-plaquette random $n_p\in\{0,1\}$ without enforcing this constraint, they include unphysical flux assignments (cubes with odd total flux) that cannot be realized by vison membranes. Consequently, the resulting hopping-phase disorder belongs to a different ensemble from the physical one, potentially shifting the mobility edge or altering the universality class.

At low spinon density and intermediate temperatures in the three-dimensional cubic-lattice $\mathbb{Z}_2$ toric code with spinon energy gap $\Delta_s$ and spinon hopping amplitude $\eta_s$, the system maps to an effective tight-binding Hamiltonian for bosonic spinons in which vison membrane occupation $n_p\in\{0,1\}$ on plaquettes $p$ induces $\pi$ fluxes through those plaquettes:
      $$
      H_{\mathrm{eff}}=\Delta_{s}\sum_{s}b_{s}^{\dagger}b_{s}-\eta_{s}\sum_{\langle s,s'\rangle}\left[\exp\!\left(iA_{ss'}\right)b_{s}^{\dagger}b_{s'}+\mathrm{H.c.}\right],
      $$
      with $(\nabla\times A)_p=\Phi_p=\pi n_p$, $A_{ss'}=-A_{s's}$, and $b_s,b_s^\dagger$ bosonic spinon operators. In this mapping the vison configuration acts as an emergent bimodal ($\pm$) sign pattern for the spinon hopping phases (equivalently plaquettes threaded by $0$ or $\pi$ flux), and the regime of interest is the Born–Oppenheimer limit where visons are quasistatic on spinon timescales.

steps.reasoning: Start from the emergent random-sign bimodal tight-binding model established previously: treat the effective Hamiltonian $H_{\mathrm{eff}}$ with plaquette fluxes $\Phi_p=\pi n_p$ as a single-particle tight-binding model for spinons hopping on the 3D cubic lattice in a stochastic $\pi$-flux background (vison-induced sign disorder).

Define the inverse participation ratio and multifractal exponent used to diagnose localization: for a normalized eigenstate $\psi_i$ at lattice site $i$ on a cubic lattice of linear size $L$ (total sites $L^3$), the generalized inverse participation ratio is $\mathrm{IPR}_q=\sum_i|\psi_i|^{2q}$ and the multifractal exponent is
$$
D_q=\frac{1}{1-q}\frac{\ln(\mathrm{IPR}_q)}{\ln L^3},
$$
so that in the thermodynamic limit $D_q\to0$ for localized states and $D_q\to1$ for extended states (for $q=\tfrac12$ and $q=2$ considered here).

Explain numerical procedure and averaging used to probe the spectrum: compute eigenstates by exact diagonalization across multiple system sizes, average over vison configurations drawn according to the emergent gauge constraints (sampling counts per system size noted in the paper), and average over a small energy shell around the target energy to obtain disorder-averaged $\overline{D_q}(E)$ as a function of energy $E$ measured in units of $\eta_s$.
[66]

Report the observed energy dependence of $\overline{D_q}$ and the identification of a mobility edge: the disorder-averaged multifractal coefficients $\overline{D_q}(E)$ (for $q=2$ and $q=\tfrac12$) show a trend toward $\overline{D_q}\approx1$ near the middle of the spectrum and $\overline{D_q}\approx0$ near the band edge, indicating extended states in the bulk and localized states in the tails; from these data the authors identify a mobility edge near $E_c/\eta_s\approx-4.35$, with $\overline{D_q}\to0$ for $|E|>|E_c|$ and $\overline{D_q}\to1$ for $|E|<|E_c|$.
Fig. 2

Perform finite-size scaling (curve collapse) of $\overline{D_q}$ to obtain more precise critical energies and a critical exponent: collapsing $\overline{D_q}(E)$ curves for different $L$ yields best-fit critical energies $E_c/\eta_s=-4.33$ for $q=2$ and $E_c/\eta_s=-4.37$ for $q=\tfrac12$, with a critical exponent $\nu\approx1.6$ describing the divergence of the correlation length near the transition; this finite-size scaling procedure follows the standard multifractal/finite-size collapse methodology for Anderson transitions.

Corroborate the mobility-edge estimate using level-spacing $r$-ratio analysis: define consecutive level gaps $\delta_n=E_n-E_{n-1}$ and the ratio $r_n=\min(\delta_n,\delta_{n-1})/\max(\delta_n,\delta_{n-1})$, recall that $\overline{r}=2\log 2-1\approx0.386$ for Poisson (localized) statistics and $\overline{r}\approx0.5295$ for GOE (extended) statistics, and observe that $\overline{r}(E)$ transitions from the Poisson value at low energies to the GOE value near the band center, with finite-size scaling of $\overline{r}$ giving a consistent critical energy $E_c/\eta_s\approx-4.37$ and critical exponent $\nu\approx1.6$.
Fig. 3

Note consistency with the orthogonal Anderson universality class: explain that the effective Hamiltonian is real and symmetric (time-reversal symmetric) so the localization transition is expected to belong to the orthogonal class; the numerically extracted critical exponent $\nu\approx1.6$ is in very good agreement with the known 3D orthogonal Anderson transition exponent $\nu_{\mathrm{AT}}\approx1.58$, supporting that the observed mobility-edge transition falls into the 3D orthogonal universality class.
[41, 42]

Summarize placement of localized versus extended states and numerical estimates: conclude that localized states occupy extreme band tails with $|E|>|E_c|$, extended states occupy $|E|<|E_c|$, and provide the numerical mobility-edge estimates $E_c/\eta_s\approx-4.35$ (with refined fits $E_c/\eta_s=-4.33$ for $q=2$ and $E_c/\eta_s=-4.37$ for $q=\tfrac12$) and the critical exponent $\nu\approx1.6$ consistent with the 3D orthogonal Anderson universality class.

motivating_questions.content: The localization properties of tight-binding particles with purely off-diagonal bimodal ($\pm$) sign disorder resulting from emergent $\pi$ fluxes in three dimensions were not known: specifically, whether a mobility edge exists (unlike 2D where all but special states are localized), how close any mobility edge would be to the band edges, and to which universality class a possible Anderson transition would belong. Prior numerical studies of off-diagonal disorder in 3D existed for other disorder ensembles, but the particular case where the sign distribution derives from a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ gauge structure and has fixed magnitude $|\exp(iA_{ss'})|=1$ had not been characterized. Without locating the mobility edge and identifying the critical exponent, one cannot predict which portion of the spectrum contributes extended states, nor classify the transition for comparison with standard Anderson models or experimental probes.

steps.reasoning: State the upstream inputs used as known: take the ARPES-derived transfer-integral mean values $t_0$ for each dimer type (from earlier experimental TB fits) and the computed absolute dynamical disorder amplitudes $\sigma_t$ for each dimer (from MD+FO-DFT) as the input parameters for the disordered tight-binding simulations.

Describe the disordered tight-binding model and sampling protocol: initialize a tight-binding lattice of $80\times80$ sites with periodic boundary conditions, connect nearest neighbors by transfer integrals sampled independently from Gaussian distributions $P(t)\propto\exp\big(-(t-t_0)^2/(2\sigma_t^2)\big)$ where $t_0$ is the ARPES mean for the given bond and $\sigma_t$ is the MD+FO-DFT standard deviation; run the model for 500 different disorder realizations and compute ensemble-averaged observables.
Fig. 3d

Define the observables computed from the disordered TB model: compute the disorder-averaged density of states (DOS) referenced to the valence-band-maximum energy $E_{\text{VBM}}$, and compute the inverse participation ratio (IPR) for each eigenstate as $\text{IPR} = \big[ \sum_i |c_i|^4 / (\sum_i |c_i|^2)^2 \big]^{-1}$ where $c_i$ are the real-space amplitudes of the eigenstate; the mean IPR as a function of energy characterizes the spatial delocalization of states.
[16]

Report the DOS simulation outcome for pentacene and picene and relate topology to DOS near the VBM: the disorder-averaged DOS shows that pentacene exhibits a large DOS close to the VBM because its frustrated transfer-integral topology produces flat bands at that energy, whereas picene exhibits a low DOS at the VBM due to its isotropic (same-sign) transfer-integral topology; at energies above $E_{\text{VBM}}$ pentacene shows pronounced tail states whereas picene shows much weaker tails.
Fig. 3d

Report the IPR results quantifying tail-state localization: the computed mean inverse participation ratio (IPR) reveals that tail states in pentacene extend up to $E - E_{\text{VBM}} \approx 50\,\text{meV}$ and have $\text{IPR} \approx 10$, indicating strong localization, whereas picene's tail states in the same relevant energy window have $\text{IPR} \approx 100$, i.e. about one order of magnitude larger indicating much more delocalized tail states; the authors present these IPR spectra and highlight the logarithmic scale used to display the large differences.
Fig. 3e

State the authors' interpretation connecting topology, disorder, and localization: the frustrated transfer-integral topology in pentacene concentrates DOS near the VBM and produces localized tail states susceptible to disorder, while picene's isotropic topology combined with smaller relative dynamical disorder yields a low DOS at the VBM and tail states that are substantially more delocalized, which the authors argue enhances resilience of valence-band-edge states relevant for thermally activated charge transport.

motivating_questions.content: The transient-localization theory identifies localization length (or IPR) near the band edge as the central quantity controlling mobility, but direct, quantitatively consistent predictions of DOS and IPR that combine experimentally determined $t_0$ and computed $\sigma_t$ for these benchmark crystals were lacking. Without such simulations it was not possible to judge whether the measured and computed differences in orbital shape and coupling statistics actually produce substantial changes in the spatial extent of states relevant to transport. This conclusion fills that gap by providing disorder simulations—anchored to ARPES and MD+FO-DFT inputs—that yield DOS and IPR results demonstrating a strong material-dependent difference in tail-state delocalization.

conclusion.content: Both the local spin-Chern marker (LSCM) and the local $\mathbb{Z}_2$ marker (LZ2M) correctly map the local topology in the presence of Anderson on-site disorder. For a disordered Kane-Mele sample with disorder amplitude $W=2$ (uniform distribution in $[-1,1]$) in a parameter regime where the single-point spin-Chern number predicts a topological phase ($\Delta/\lambda_{SO}=0.5$, $\lambda_R/\lambda_{SO}=1$), the periodic-boundary-condition (PBC) and open-boundary-condition (OBC) markers, after an appropriate local averaging radius $R=3$ (in lattice constant units), recover the expected topological bulk signal and show boundary and interface signatures consistent with metallic edge states.

premises.content: The robustness of the local $\mathbb{Z}_2$ markers to Anderson disorder is tested only on the Kane-Mele model with Anderson on-site disorder of amplitude $W=2$ (uniform distribution in $[-1,1]$), for a single set of parameters in the topological phase ($\Delta/\lambda_{SO}=0.5$, $\lambda_R/\lambda_{SO}=1$) and with a macroscopic averaging radius $R=3$ (in units of the lattice parameter). Here $\Delta$ is the staggered on-site potential, $\lambda_{SO}$ is the intrinsic spin-orbit coupling strength, $\lambda_R$ is the Rashba spin-orbit coupling strength, and $W$ is the disorder amplitude. No tests are performed for other disorder strengths, different disorder types (e.g., off-diagonal disorder, bond disorder, disorder in the spin-orbit coupling), or in the trivial phase near the transition. The behavior under stronger disorder that may close the mobility gap or induce an Anderson topological transition is not examined.

premises.content: For a two-dimensional system with open boundary conditions, the local spin-Chern marker (LSCM) $\nu(\mathbf{r})$ is defined as follows. Let $\mathcal{P}$ be the projector onto the $N_{occ}$ occupied eigenstates of the Hamiltonian. Diagonalize the projected spin operator $\mathcal{P}S_z\mathcal{P}$, where $S_z$ is the $z$-component of the spin operator, to obtain eigenvalues $s_\lambda$ and eigenvectors $|\phi_{\lambda}\rangle$. Construct projectors onto positive and negative spin sectors: $\mathcal{P}_\sigma = \sum_{\lambda: \mathrm{sgn}(s_\lambda)=\sigma} |\phi_{\lambda}\rangle\langle\phi_{\lambda}|$ for $\sigma = \pm$. Compute the individual local Chern markers $\mathfrak{C}_\sigma(\mathbf{r}) = 4\pi \Im \langle\mathbf{r}| \mathcal{P}_\sigma [x,\mathcal{P}_\sigma] [y,\mathcal{P}_\sigma] |\mathbf{r}\rangle$, where $\Im$ denotes the imaginary part, $x$ and $y$ are the Cartesian components of the position operator $\mathbf{r}$, and $|\mathbf{r}\rangle$ is a position eigenstate. The local $\mathbb{Z}_2$ marker is then $\nu(\mathbf{r}) = (\mathfrak{C}_+(\mathbf{r}) - \mathfrak{C}_-(\mathbf{r}))/2 \mod 2$.

premises.title: Local OBC spin‑Chern marker (LSCM) definition

premises.content: For a two-dimensional system with open boundary conditions, the local $\mathbb{Z}_2$ marker based solely on time-reversal (TR) symmetry (LZ2M) is defined as follows. Let $\mathcal{P}$ be the projector onto the $N_{occ}$ occupied eigenstates $|\psi_m\rangle$ of the Hamiltonian. Split the occupied Hilbert space into two subspaces that are conjugate under the antiunitary time-reversal operator $\Theta$ (satisfying $\Theta^2 = -1$ for spin-1/2). This is achieved by constructing quasi-Wannier functions (qWFs) via projection onto trial orbitals $|g_n\rangle$ that break TR symmetry: $|\phi_n\rangle = \sum_m |\psi_m\rangle\langle\psi_m|g_n\rangle$, orthonormalization using the overlap matrix $S_{mn} = \langle\phi_m|\phi_n\rangle$ to obtain $|\tilde{w}_n\rangle = \sum_m |\phi_m\rangle S^{-1}_{mn}$, and then taking half of the resulting states (one from each Kramers pair) to define projectors $\mathcal{P}_1$ and $\mathcal{P}_2$ onto the two subspaces. Compute the individual local Chern markers $\mathfrak{C}_i(\mathbf{r}) = 4\pi \Im \langle\mathbf{r}| \mathcal{P}_i [x,\mathcal{P}_i] [y,\mathcal{P}_i] |\mathbf{r}\rangle$ for $i=1,2$, where $\Im$ denotes the imaginary part, $x$ and $y$ are the Cartesian components of the position operator $\mathbf{r}$, and $|\mathbf{r}\rangle$ is a position eigenstate. The local $\mathbb{Z}_2$ marker is then $\Delta(\mathbf{r}) = (\mathfrak{C}_1(\mathbf{r}) - \mathfrak{C}_2(\mathbf{r}))/2 \mod 2$.

The bilayer Lieb-lattice tight-binding Hamiltonian for a two-layer system with a layer-index pseudospin $\mu\in\{-1,1\}$ is given by
      $$
      H=\sum_{i,\mu}U_{i,\mu}\,c_{i,\mu}^{\dagger}c_{i,\mu}+t_0\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle,\mu}c_{i,\mu}^{\dagger}c_{j,\mu}+t_c\sum_{\langle\langle i,j\rangle\rangle,\mu}\left\{\frac{\mu(\mathbf{n}_{ij}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{e}_z)+1}{2}\right\}c_{i,\mu}^{\dagger}c_{j,-\mu},
      $$
      where $c_{i,\mu}^{\dagger}$ ($c_{i,\mu}$) creates (annihilates) an excitation on site $i$ in layer $\mu$, $U_{i,\mu}$ is the on-site energy for sublattice sites A, B, C in layer $\mu$, $t_0$ is the intralayer nearest-neighbor coupling strength, $t_c$ is the chiral interlayer next-nearest-neighbor coupling strength, and $\mathbf{n}_{ij}=\mathbf{e}_{ik}\times\mathbf{e}_{kj}$ with $k$ the intermediate site between $i$ and $j$. The layer Pauli matrix $\sigma_y$ yields the layer pseudospin operator $\tau_y=\sigma_y\otimes I_N$ (with $N$ the number of intralayer atoms); because $[H,\tau_y]\neq0$ the pseudospin is not conserved. In this model, the chiral interlayer coupling $t_c$ acts as a synthetic spin-orbit coupling that opens topologically nontrivial bandgaps for the lower bands, allowing characterization of phases by the spin Chern number $C_s=(C_+-C_-)/2$. The model thus provides a microscopic Hamiltonian that encodes (i) a bilayer pseudospin degree of freedom, (ii) spin-nonconserving dynamics, and (iii) a chiral interlayer term that can produce spin-dependent helical edge modes.

A real-space topological invariant for the spin sector is formulated and employed. First, define the projector onto occupied states below the lower bandgap (the gap between the lower two bulk bands) as $P=\sum_{i}^{N_{\mathrm{occ}}}|\psi_i\rangle\langle\psi_i|$ where $N_{\mathrm{occ}}=2N_xN_y$ with $N_x$ and $N_y$ the number of unit cells in the $x$ and $y$ spatial directions. Next, project into the pseudospin space (the layer degree of freedom) using $P_y=P\tau_yP$ where $\tau_y=\sigma_y\otimes I_N$, $\sigma_y$ is the Pauli matrix for the layer pseudospin, $I_N$ is the identity matrix of size $N=3N_xN_y$ (the total number of intralayer atoms). The eigenproblem of $P_y$ is $P_y|\pm\varphi_i\rangle=S_{\pm}|\pm\varphi_i\rangle$ with eigenvalues $S_{\pm}=\pm\hbar/2$, and the eigenvectors yield projectors onto pseudospin-up and -down occupied states: $P_{\pm}=\sum_{i}^{N_{\mathrm{occ}}/2}|\pm\varphi_i\rangle\langle\pm\varphi_i|$. Then construct projected position operators $U_{\pm}=P_{\pm}e^{i2\pi X}P_{\pm}$ and $V_{\pm}=P_{\pm}e^{i2\pi Y}P_{\pm}$, where $X$ and $Y$ are diagonal matrices of atomic coordinates normalized to the unit cell. The spin Bott indices for each pseudospin are
      $$
      B_{\pm}=\frac{1}{2\pi}\operatorname{Im}\left\{ \mathrm{tr}\left[\log\left(\widetilde{V}_{\pm}\widetilde{U}_{\pm}\widetilde{V}_{\pm}^{\dagger}\widetilde{U}_{\pm}^{\dagger}\right)\right]\right\},
      $$
      and the spin Bott index is $B_s=\frac{1}{2}(B_+ - B_-)$. This real-space invariant is applied to disordered supercells to identify trivial ($B_s=0$) and disorder-induced topological ($B_s=1$) regimes. The method requires an absolute spectral gap (a range of frequencies with no eigenstates) for reliable computation; without an absolute gap the Bott-index calculation may be inaccurate.

Introduce uniformly distributed random on-site disorder $\delta U$ at every atomic site in the supercell with $\delta U\in[-w/2,w/2]$, where $w$ is the disorder strength parameter. motivating_questions.content: To establish that disorder can induce topology in a TRS-preserving, spin-nonconserving lattice one must show a mechanism by which a trivial bulk spectrum becomes topological when randomness is introduced, and one must identify numerically observable signatures of that transition in realistic finite samples. Previously, most observed TAI phenomena were restricted to TRS-breaking systems or low-dimensional/engineered setups; it was unclear whether a two-dimensional TRS-preserving model with layer pseudospin and nonconserved spin would exhibit a disorder-driven trivial-to-topological transition in finite-size, experimentally realizable supercells. Moreover, in disordered systems band structures are ill-defined, so one must demonstrate the transition via eigenvalue spectra and boundary eigenstates in finite supercells with appropriate boundary conditions. The numerical results above directly address these gaps by (i) showing closure and reopening of the lower gap induced by on-site disorder in a realistic-size supercell, and (ii) producing boundary-localized mid-gap states under HBC that serve as the finite-size signature of a TAI phase in a spin-nonconserving TRS-preserving model.

steps.reasoning:
Define the non-interacting tight-binding model and the numerical procedure: consider the tight-binding Hamiltonian
$H=-t\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle} c_i^\dagger c_j + \mathrm{H.c.} + \sum_i W_i c_i^\dagger c_i$,
where $t$ is the hopping amplitude, $W_i$ the on-site disorder potential, the lattice spacing is $a$, system size is $N=10000$ sites (so $\Omega=Na$), and exact diagonalization is used to obtain single-particle eigenstates for each disorder realization; averages are performed over $1000$ independent disorder realizations.

Define disorder strength measure and localization-length estimator: characterize the disorder strength by the zero-distance correlation $D=\overline{W(x)W(x)}=\frac{W_0^2 k_c}{2\pi}$ (with the chosen cutoff $k_c=\frac{\pi}{2a}$ in the numerical study), compute the inverse participation ratio $\mathrm{IPR}=\int dx\,|\psi(x)|^{4}$ for eigenstates, and use the weak-disorder relation $\mathrm{IPR}=1/\xi$ to extract a localization length $\xi$ for states in an energy bin.

Describe the types of disorder generated and how they are produced numerically: generate three disorder models that share the same second-moment cutoff at $k_{c}=2k_{\mathrm{F}}$: blue-detuned speckle disorder (BSD), red-detuned speckle disorder (RSD), and Gaussian colored disorder (GCD) constructed to have the same two-point correlation; BSD and RSD are produced from the squared modulus of a complex Gaussian electric field (including non-Gaussian and odd-moment features for BSD/RSD), while GCD is directly sampled as a Gaussian random field in Fourier space with spectrum $A_k=W_0^{2}(1-|k|/k_c)$ and inverse Fourier transformed to real space. The numerical generation procedures follow the methods summarized in the Supplementary Material.
Supplementary Material

Present the numerical findings for $k_{\mathrm{F}}=k_{c}/2$ and identify the deviation from white-noise scaling: plotting the extracted localization length $\xi$ versus disorder strength $D$ for eigenstates at momentum corresponding to $k_{\mathrm{F}}=k_{c}/2$ shows that all three disorder types deviate from the white-noise prediction $\xi\propto D^{-1}$. In particular, the GCD and RSD data in the weak-disorder regime exhibit a clear scaling compatible with $\xi\propto D^{-3/2}$ over the accessible range before finite-size effects (saturation at system size $N=10000$) or the onset of strong-disorder behavior limit the scaling range; BSD displays a crossover behavior that is consistent with approaching the same $D^{-3/2}$ exponent at weak disorder. These numerical trends are shown and compared to guide-to-eye power laws in the plotted data.

Note the limitations and the relation to perturbative RG: emphasize that the observed $\xi\propto D^{-3/2}$ scaling is unexpected from the perturbative RG analysis presented earlier (which does not predict such an exponent) and that the numerical observation holds before finite-size and strong-disorder effects set in; the authors state that the origin of this $D^{-3/2}$ scaling is not understood in the present theoretical framework and requires further numerical and theoretical investigation.

motivating_questions.content: The scaling of the single-particle localization length $\xi$ with disorder intensity $D$ is well-known for uncorrelated (white-noise) disorder ($\xi\propto D^{-1}$ in the regimes considered), and diagrammatic/single-particle theories can predict scaling when the disorder spectral content at $2k_{\mathrm{F}}$ is finite. However, when the disorder spectral weight vanishes at $2k_{\mathrm{F}}$ (as for speckle-like correlations with $k_c=2k_{\mathrm{F}}$), higher-order processes in the disorder and non-Gaussian statistical moments (as in BSD/RSD) can alter scaling laws. Prior to these simulations there was no concrete numerical characterization of $\xi(D)$ for non-interacting fermions at the critical spectral-cutoff condition, so there was no basis to test whether the naive expectation (that higher-order terms produce at least $\xi\propto D^{-2}$ or restore white-noise scaling) holds. Quantitative numerical data are necessary to uncover any anomalous scaling and to guide theoretical efforts toward understanding such deviations.

premises.content:
The spectral projector $P=\theta(\epsilon-H)$ at zero temperature can be approximated by a finite-order Chebyshev (kernel polynomial method, KPM) expansion of the Hamiltonian $H$ rescaled so that its spectrum lies in $[-1,1]$, namely
      $$
      P(\epsilon,H)=\sum_{m=0}^{M}g_{m}\,\mu_{m}(\epsilon)\,T_{m}(H),
      $$
      where $T_{m}(H)$ is the $m^{\text{th}}$ Chebyshev polynomial of the (rescaled) Hamiltonian, $g_{m}$ is a damping kernel factor, and the Chebyshev moments $\mu_{m}(\epsilon)$ for the step function at Fermi parameter $\epsilon$ are given explicitly by
      $$
      \mu_{m}(\epsilon)=\begin{cases}
      1-\dfrac{\cos^{-1}(\epsilon)}{\pi}, & m=0,\\[6pt]
      -\dfrac{2\sin\!\big(\cos^{-1}(\epsilon)\big)}{m\pi}, & m\neq 0,
      \end{cases}
      $$
      for the filled-state projector $P$, and similarly with sign-reversed $m\neq 0$ moments for the complementary projector $Q=1-P$:
      $$
      \mu_{m}^{(Q)}(\epsilon)=\begin{cases}
      1-\dfrac{\cos^{-1}(\epsilon)}{\pi}, & m=0,\\[6pt]
      \dfrac{2\sin\!\big(\cos^{-1}(\epsilon)\big)}{m\pi}, & m\neq 0.
      \end{cases}
      $$
      These formulas define how to obtain the projectors entering the universal topological operator
      $$
      \hat{\mathcal{C}}=N_{D}W\big[Q\hat{r}_{1}P\hat{r}_{2}\cdots\hat{r}_{D}\mathcal{O}+(-1)^{D+1}P\hat{r}_{1}Q\hat{r}_{2}\cdots\hat{r}_{D}\overline{\mathcal{O}}\big],
      $$
      by replacing $P$ and $Q$ with their KPM expansions and then evaluating the resulting operator action on basis vectors using the Chebyshev recurrence.

steps.reasoning:
Adopt the three-dimensional time-reversal-symmetric tight-binding Dirac model: define the momentum-space Hamiltonian $H_{0}(\mathbf{k})$ as
$
H_{0}(\mathbf{k})=(M_{0}+4M_{2}+2M_{1})\Gamma^{5}-2\big(M_{1}\cos k_{z}+M_{2}(\cos k_{x}+\cos k_{y})\big)\Gamma^{5}+B_{0}\sin k_{z}\Gamma^{4}+A_{0}\big(\sin k_{y}\Gamma^{1}-\sin k_{x}\Gamma^{2}\big),
$
where $\Gamma^{1\ldots5}$ are $4\times4$ gamma matrices and the convention used is $\Gamma^{1}=\sigma_{x}\tau_{x},\Gamma^{2}=\sigma_{y}\tau_{x},\Gamma^{3}=\sigma_{z}\tau_{x},\Gamma^{4}=\sigma_{0}\tau_{y},\Gamma^{5}=\sigma_{0}\tau_{z}$, with $\sigma_{i}$ and $\tau_{i}$ denoting Pauli matrices acting on spin and orbital subspaces respectively; $M_{0},M_{1},M_{2},A_{0},B_{0}$ are model parameters. A topological phase transition occurs at $M_{0}=0$.

Define the four impurity operators that modify nonzero matrix elements of the lattice Hamiltonian in real space, where $|\mathbf{r}\rangle\langle\mathbf{r}'|$ denotes a hopping or onsite projector between lattice sites and $\otimes$ denotes tensor product with the internal gamma-matrix space:
$
H_{\mathrm{imp}}^{1}=M_{\mathrm{imp}}|\mathbf{r}\rangle\langle\mathbf{r}|\otimes\Gamma^{5},
$
$
H_{\mathrm{imp}}^{2}=A_{\mathrm{imp}}|\mathbf{r}\rangle\langle\mathbf{r}+a\hat{y}|\otimes\Gamma^{1}+\mathrm{h.c.},
$
$
H_{\mathrm{imp}}^{3}=A_{\mathrm{imp}}|\mathbf{r}\rangle\langle\mathbf{r}+a\hat{x}|\otimes\Gamma^{2}+\mathrm{h.c.},
$
$
H_{\mathrm{imp}}^{4}=B_{\mathrm{imp}}|\mathbf{r}\rangle\langle\mathbf{r}+a\hat{z}|\otimes\Gamma^{4}+\mathrm{h.c.},
$
where $a$ denotes the lattice spacing, $M_{\mathrm{imp}}$, $A_{\mathrm{imp}}$, $B_{\mathrm{imp}}$ denote impurity strengths, and $\mathrm{h.c.}$ denotes the Hermitian conjugate of the hopping term.

Define the change in the spatially averaged marker induced by an impurity: compute the impurity-perturbed average marker $\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{imp}}$ by summing the local marker $\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{r})$ over sites in a central $10\times10\times10$ cube in a sample of linear size $L$,
$
\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{imp}}=\sum_{\mathbf{r}}\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{r}),
$
where the sum is over the sites inside the central cube and the impurity is placed at the cube center; define the change $\Delta C=\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{clean}}-\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{imp}}$, where $\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{clean}}$ denotes the average marker for the clean system without impurity.

Describe the numerical experiments and parameter choices used to probe these impurities: the simulations used KPM with Chebyshev expansion order 800 and representative impurity parameters of order-unity strengths (for example, the paper reports $M_{\mathrm{imp}}=M_{S_{x}}=4$, $A_{\mathrm{imp}}=B_{\mathrm{imp}}=3$, $t_{\mathrm{imp}}=1$ for the illustrative runs), and computed $\Delta C$ as a function of inverse system volume $1/L^{3}$ to test the thermodynamic limit $1/L^{3}\to0$. Fig. 1

Report the numerical observation for nonzero-element impurities: the data plotted for $\Delta C$ versus $1/L^{3}$ for the four impurity types $H_{\mathrm{imp}}^{1},H_{\mathrm{imp}}^{2},H_{\mathrm{imp}}^{3},H_{\mathrm{imp}}^{4}$ (displayed in Fig. 1 panels corresponding to these impurity types) show that $\Delta C$ decreases with system size and extrapolates to approximately zero as $1/L^{3}\rightarrow 0$, within numerical precision; the figure caption indicates these panels correspond to impurities varying non-zero elements and the red vertical bars denote the error in the extrapolated value. Fig. 1

Conclude that nonzero-element impurities preserve the spatially averaged marker in the thermodynamic limit: because $\Delta C$ extrapolates to zero with $1/L^{3}\to0$ for the examined nonzero-element impurity types and parameter values, the spatially averaged marker is numerically observed to be unchanged by these impurities in the thermodynamic limit for the parameters studied, indicating that these impurity types do not alter the global (spatially averaged) topological marker as $L\to\infty$.

motivating_questions.content: Experimentally and theoretically it is important to know which local perturbations preserve bulk topological quantization when disorder is present. In one and two dimensions there exist perturbative analytic proofs that dilute impurities modifying nonzero Hamiltonian matrix elements preserve the averaged marker; in three dimensions this analytic characterization was lacking. If impurities of the nonzero-matrix-element type did alter the averaged marker in 3D, then quantitative predictions for realistic materials (e.g., $Bi_{2}Se_{3}$) would require knowledge of impurity composition and would complicate the notion of robust bulk topology. The numerical evidence reported here addresses this gap by testing representative nonzero-element impurity operators in a lattice regularization of a 3D class AII Dirac model and showing that the averaged marker change vanishes as system volume increases, thereby providing the missing three-dimensional numerical evidence for robustness against this class of perturbations.

Using the mean-field one-dimensional charge-density-wave (CDW) tight-binding Hamiltonian
      $H = -t\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}\left(c_{j}^{\dagger}c_{j+1}+c_{j+1}^{\dagger}c_{j}\right) + V\sum_{j=1}^{N-1} c_{j}^{\dagger} c_{j}\, c_{j+1}^{\dagger} c_{j+1} + \sum_{j=1}^{N}\zeta_{j} c_{j}^{\dagger} c_{j}$,
      with $t>0$ the nearest-neighbour tunnelling amplitude, $V$ the nearest-neighbour Coulomb interaction, $\zeta_{j}$ a (possibly zero) on-site impurity potential, and with the CDW phase parameter $\phi$ entering the mean-field density modulation $A\cos(Qja+\phi)$ (with propagation vector $Q=2\pi n/a$), the family of CDW Hamiltonians parametrised by $\phi$ maps one-to-one onto the Landau-gauge Hofstadter/IQHE problem (identifications $k\!\to\!k_x$, $Q\!\to\!eB/(hc)$, $\phi\!\to\!k_y a$). Exploiting this gauge-free 1D representation, numerically computed spectra and real-space eigenfunctions for the example parameters $n=1/3$, $N=63$, and $AV/t=5$ show explicitly how the highest occupied single-particle eigenstate evolves continuously as $\phi$ is varied: at $\phi=0$ the highest occupied state is localised at the right edge; for $\pi/3\lesssim\phi\lesssim\pi$ it becomes a bulk “particle-in-a-box”–like state; for $\pi\lesssim\phi\lesssim 5\pi/3$ it is localised at the left edge; and at $\phi\simeq 5\pi/3$ it switches discontinuously back to a right-edge state. This provides a gauge-independent, real-space visualisation of edge-to-edge charge transfer equivalent to Laughlin’s flux-threading / Thouless pumping process.

By choosing Raman frequencies $\nu_{\pm,\cdot}$ and two-step Rabi-frequency products $\Omega_{ne}^{(+)}\Omega_{en'}^{(-)}$ so that $\nu_{+,n}-\nu_{-,n'}+\omega_n^{(g)}-\omega_{n'}^{(g)}=\text{const.}$ and $J_{nn'}=J=\text{const.}$, where $J_{nn'}\simeq\hbar\Omega_{ne}^{(+)}\Omega_{en'}^{(-)}/[\nu_{+,n}-(\omega^{(e)}-\omega_n^{(g)})]$ is the off-diagonal coupling between states $|\vec{k}_n,n\rangle_g$ and $|\vec{k}_{n'},n'\rangle_g$, and by controlling the momentum transfers $\hbar(\vec{q}_{+,n}-\vec{q}_{-,n'})$, the Raman-coupled system of long-lived states $|\vec{k}_n,n\rangle_g$ (with momentum $\hbar\vec{k}_n$ and internal energy $\hbar\omega_n^{(g)}$) reduces to an effective tight-binding Hamiltonian in the entangled basis $|\vec{k}_i,i\rangle$ of size $N$,
      $$
      H=\begin{pmatrix}
      E_1 & -J & 0 & \cdots & -J\\
      -J & E_2 & -J & \cdots & 0\\
      0 & -J & E_3 & \ddots & \vdots\\
      \vdots & & \ddots & \ddots & -J\\
      -J & 0 & \cdots & -J & E_N
      \end{pmatrix},
      $$
      where the diagonal energies $E_n$ may be set identical (ordered lattice) or drawn from a flat random distribution $E_n\in[-\Delta/2,\Delta/2]$ (disordered lattice). Off-diagonal connectivity (i.e., which $J_{nn'}$ are nonzero) is engineered by selecting which pairs of levels are Raman-resonantly coupled: coupling only nearest-index pairs realizes an effective 1D momentum-space lattice; adding couplings to two additional index offsets realizes 2D or 3D connectivities (each site having 2, 4, or 6 neighbors respectively); coupling every level to a single initially populated level realizes an effective infinite-dimensional ($\infty$D-like) connectivity for the remaining subspace.

steps.reasoning: Treat the mapping to a tight-binding Hamiltonian with controllable diagonal disorder and engineered connectivity (Conclusion 2) as known; recall the symbols $N$ for system size (number of entangled momentum-internal sites), $J$ for uniform off-diagonal coupling strength, and $\Delta$ for the width of the flat on-site-energy random distribution $E_n\in[-\Delta/2,\Delta/2]$.

State the well-known result invoked by the authors for Anderson-type models (as cited): for truly uncorrelated random diagonal disorder in one dimension (1D) any nonzero disorder causes localization in the thermodynamic limit $N\to\infty$; define ``localization'' here as eigenstates being spatially (here momentum-space) exponentially localized rather than extended. Cite the authors' reference for this established result.

Explain the finite-size effect the authors identify: for finite $N$ there appears an artificial localization crossover characterized by a finite characteristic disorder ratio $(\Delta/J)_C$ (the disorder strength at which the ground-state momentum distribution changes qualitatively), but as $N\to\infty$ this characteristic crossover point flows toward zero in 1D (and, as stated by the authors, also in 2D), meaning $(\Delta/J)_C\to0$. Cite the authors' numerical flow plot demonstrating $(\Delta/J)_C$ versus $N$ that shows this behavior.

Describe the 3D case as treated by the authors: when the engineered connectivity makes each site have six neighbors (effective 3D lattice), the system exhibits a true localization transition at a finite critical disorder strength $(\Delta/J)_C$ in the thermodynamic limit; the authors extract this critical value from finite-size scaling of their numerical model and report that $(\Delta/J)_C$ flows toward roughly $10$ as $N\to\infty$, as shown by their plot of the crossover point versus $N$.

Explain the effective infinite-dimensional ($\infty$D-like) connectivity case: by coupling every level to a single initially populated level the remaining subspace behaves analogously to an infinite-dimensional Anderson model in which there is no localization phase transition; the authors state that in this case the crossover point flows to infinity with system size (more precisely it scales with $N$), i.e., $(\Delta/J)_C\to\infty$ as $N\to\infty$, and they display this scaling in their numerical plot.

Address quasiperiodic (Aubry–André-type) diagonal perturbations in 1D: start from the same tight-binding mapping (Conclusion 2) but replace the uncorrelated random $E_n$ by a quasiperiodic modulation of the diagonal energies; state the known theoretical result invoked by the authors that a 1D quasiperiodic (Aubry–André) model exhibits a true localization transition at the critical value $(\Delta/J)_C=2$, and note that the authors' finite-size scaling of their proposed momentum-space realization shows flow toward this critical value as $N\to\infty$.

Summarize the dimension-and-disorder-class-dependent behaviors the authors predict for the TIE-implemented momentum-space Anderson problem: (i) 1D (and 2D) with true uncorrelated random disorder has no finite critical disorder in the thermodynamic limit, with the apparent finite-$N$ crossover point flowing to zero [numerics in Fig. 3(b)]; (ii) 3D displays a true localization transition at finite $(\Delta/J)_C$ which the authors' finite-size scaling suggests flows to $\simeq10$ as $N\to\infty$ [Fig. 3(c)]; (iii) an $\infty$D-like connectivity yields no thermodynamic transition because the crossover point scales to infinity with $N$ [Fig. 3(d)]; and (iv) 1D quasiperiodic (Aubry–André) diagonal perturbations produce a true transition at $(\Delta/J)_C=2$, with finite-size scaling flowing to this value [Fig. 3(b)].

motivating_questions.content: The central unresolved physical question is how the standard Anderson localization phenomenology — specifically the existence or absence of a localization-delocalization transition and the critical disorder strength — translates to momentum-space lattices constructed from entangled momentum-internal states: does the known dimensional dependence (all states localized in 1D/2D; transition in 3D) hold when the "sites" correspond to momentum-internal states coupled by Raman processes, and how do finite system size and the specific form of diagonal perturbations (true random disorder versus quasiperiodic modulation) influence observable crossovers? Prior to this work there were no quantitative predictions tying achievable Raman-coupling Hamiltonians to the presence or absence of a thermodynamic localization transition in momentum space, nor finite-size scaling data indicating the flow of the apparent crossover point $(\Delta/J)_C$ for realizable system sizes. This gap prevented designing experiments to distinguish finite-size crossovers from true phase transitions and to predict the disorder strength required to observe localization in practicable setups.
